Adder
AD-er
noun
From the Saxon naedre, a serpent, the initial n lost by wearing into the article (a naddre becoming an adder); in the Authorized Version it renders several Hebrew words for the venomous snake — shephiphon, the horned viper of the path (Gen 49:17); pethen, the deaf asp of Psa 58:4; 'akshub, the swelling adder of Psa 140:3; and tsiph'oni, the biting adder of Pro 23:32.

Biblical Definition

The adder is the venomous serpent of the Authorized Version, the small death that lies in the road. Jacob’s blessing on Dan sets it in the dust of the path, a serpent by the way that bites the horse heels so that the rider falls backward (Gen 49:17) — a picture of a small enemy bringing down a great one from below. Solomon lays it at the bottom of the wine cup: what goes down smooth and red “at the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder” (Pro 23:32). But the adder’s greatest doctrinal weight lies in Psa 58:4, where the wicked are “like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.” That is total depravity drawn to the life. The charmer’s art is not lacking; the ear is. The man dead in trespasses is not merely uninstructed, so that better argument would move him; he is unresponsive, and stops the ear against the very sweetness that would save. Persuasion alone cannot raise him. Nothing short of effectual grace — the sovereign call that gives the ear it commands — will do. And over against that stands the promise: “Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder” (Psa 91:13), which is the ancient word of Gen 3:15 coming true, the Seed of the woman bruising the serpent’s head and setting the heel of His people upon the whole venomous brood.

Webster 1828 Definition

A venomous serpent or viper; in Scripture the emblem of poison hidden in the path, and of the ear that will not hear.

ADDER, a venomous serpent or viper of the smaller kind.

From the Saxon naedre, a serpent; the n was lost into the article.

Rendering several Hebrew words for venomous snakes of different sorts.

Figuratively, secret malice: “adders’ poison is under their lips” (Psa 140:3).

Figuratively, the sting hidden at the bottom of pleasure (Pro 23:32).

Key Scripture

Psa 58:4 — "Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear;"

Psa 91:13 — "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet."

Pro 23:32 — "At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder."

Psa 140:3 — "They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah."

Modern Corruption

The deaf adder is made an argument for better technique, as though the unconverted needed only a wiser charmer rather than a new ear.

expand to see more

The live misuse of Psa 58:4 is to read the deaf adder as a challenge to the charmer’s skill. If the method were sharpened, the music improved, the appeal made warmer or the argument tighter, then surely the ear would open. Whole systems of persuasion have been built on that assumption, and they mistake the psalm exactly backwards. The psalm does not fault the charming; it says the charming was done never so wisely and the ear was stopped anyway. The defect is not in the sound but in the hearer. Man by nature is not a neutral party weighing evidence; he is a stopped ear, and stops it himself, willingly, against the sweetest voice in the world.

Recover the doctrine and the labour is not abandoned but relocated. The charmer still charms — preaching remains the appointed means, and no man is excused from pleading with sinners as though their souls hung on the pleading, for they do. But the preacher no longer preaches as a man with a technique; he preaches as a man begging God to give the ear he is speaking into. Effectual calling is not preaching made more effective; it is the Spirit doing sovereignly what no eloquence can do, opening what was shut. And that is why Psa 91:13 belongs beside Psa 58:4. The adder is not negotiated with. It is trodden down, by the Seed of the woman promised in Gen 3:15, whose heel is bruised and whose foot is on the serpent’s head.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A venomous serpent of the path; in the Psalms the deaf ear of the wicked and the head beneath the believer’s heel.

expand to see more

Adder — Saxon naedre, a serpent; the n worn away into the article.

Renders shephiphon, pethen, 'akshub, and tsiph'oni — venomous snakes of several sorts.

Gen 49:17: an adder in the path that bites the heels and fells the rider.

Psa 58:4: the deaf adder stops her ear against the wisest charming — depravity, not ignorance.

Psa 91:13: the adder trodden under foot, answering the promise of Gen 3:15.

Usage

"A small enemy in the dust may bring down a great rider (Gen 49:17)."

"The sting is at the last, not at the first — that is the adder in the cup (Pro 23:32)."

"The deaf adder needs a new ear, not a better charmer."
